content.content:
# Proving Ground runs

English | [中文](README.zh.md)

Records of real Proving Ground runs: the district's certified measurements of one implementer on registered environments, kept exactly as the harness folded and exported them. A run directory is the output of one fleet plan: the cell session logs, the exported session facts, the curator-gated trajectory export, the observatory snapshot and page, the driver's report, and a manifest with every file's digest. Nothing in a run directory is edited after the run; the table below is read from those files.

## Layout

```
data/proving-ground/
  <date>-<implementer>-run-<n>/
    manifest.json        repository head, composition, implementer, session ids, per-file bytes and SHA-256
    result.json          the driver's report: fleet report, delegation records, export reports, observatory document
    facts.jsonl          scorekeeper facts, one per cell session
    trajectories.jsonl   curator-gated trajectory export, one per exported session
    observatory.json     the observatory snapshot the page was rendered from
    observatory.html     the rendered observatory page
    sessions/            the cell session logs, one JSONL file per cell, named by session id
  folds/<date>-<candidate>-against-<baseline>-<tier>.json   an offline paired fold of two recorded fleets that differ by a composition overlay, or a counterfactual of one recorded fleet re-read under a cap
  folds/<date>-<reading>-<tier>-seed<seed>.json             an offline reading over recorded arms that share a tier and seed: the routing reading (oracle and cascades over single-model arms) or the repeatability of one arm across its runs
  datasets/<name>/                                          one fold of every record's trajectories into train.jsonl, heldout.jsonl, and a manifest of the counts, distributions, digests, and the data-use purpose it was filtered for (see its own README)
  dashboard.html                                            the Proving Ground dashboard, one self-contained page folded from every record and fold above by tools/build-dashboard.mjs
  dashboard.png                                             that page at desktop width as it stood when it was last rebuilt, the image the repository's front page shows
  improvement-log.md                                        one row per improvement iteration: the change proposed, the record or fold that tested it, the paired reading, and the decision taken
  loop/ledger.jsonl                                         one JSON line per `bench loop` iteration, written by the loop and never by hand: the queue and position, the plan and overlay, the record it wrote, the verdict, delta, interval and per-arm certificates read back from that record, and the decision the fixed rule took
  loop/preflight.jsonl                                      one JSON line per run of tools/preflight.mjs, the nightly Routine's first step: the install, the build, the Claude Code CLI and its login, and the queue's dry run, each with its exit status and seconds, and the step that stopped the run, by failing or by running past its timeout, with the end of its output
```

## Running one

A run is a Loader-booted composition under `examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/` driven from an empty directory outside the repository; the driver creates the session store there and writes the exports next to it. The first run used the composition below, with the host's own Claude Code installation and account as the implementer of every cell:

```sh
mkdir -p /tmp/proving-ground-run && cd /tmp/proving-ground-run
REPO=/path/to/deepseek-harness
TSX_TSCONFIG_PATH=$REPO/tsconfig.json node --import $REPO/node_modules/tsx/dist/esm/index.mjs $REPO/examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/village-claude-implementer/driver.ts $REPO/examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/village-claude-implementer/cordis.yml > stdout.jsonl
```

Then record it, which copies the exports, every session log, and the driver's result into a new run directory, writes its `manifest.json` with the repository head, the composition, the implementers read from the run stamps, and every file's digest, and refuses to overwrite a recorded run; add a row below afterwards:

```sh
node data/proving-ground/tools/record-run.mjs /tmp/proving-ground-run 2026-09-06-claude-code-run-2 --composition examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/village-live/cordis.yml
```

A live district (`examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/village-live/`) is recorded the same way from the directory its driver runs in, one slot per run directory: the shift ledger session lands beside the cell sessions and `result.json` holds the driver's status.

## What a row proves

A delegated cell's certificate proves that the runner authored the standard before any work started, restored the immutable paths from the fixture over the tree the external agent left, found the check-owned set unchanged, and ran the checks itself. It proves nothing about how the work was done: the external agent's prompts, tool calls, and reasoning stay in its own product, so the cell session holds the stamp, the standard, the delegation records, the runs, and the certificate, and no assistant turn. The exported trajectory therefore carries no step. It is a measurement, not training data, and the `implementer` field on the stamp is what a curated export filters on. The [external implementer note](../../.agents/notes/proposed/architecture/2026-09-06-external-implementer.md) owns these rules.

## What a cell reached outside its workspace

Every record here ran its cells in a sibling layout — each cell workspace directly under the run directory, beside `plan.json`, the run log, and every other cell of the same fleet — and the records dated 2026-09-08 and earlier ran them unconfined, so nothing stopped a cell from reading any of it. [`tools/census-escapes.mjs`](tools/census-escapes.mjs) reads one record and reports, per cell, the tool calls whose path arguments name the run directory or another cell and the reads the barrier refused; [`tools/record-run.mjs`](tools/record-run.mjs) prints that census, and the per-arm totals below, with every record it writes; a run whose driver died before writing its result is recorded with `--partial <reason>`, which keeps its session logs, states only the reason in its `result.json`, and leaves any verdict to an offline fold under `folds/`. [`tools/summarize-run.mjs`](tools/summarize-run.mjs) reads one record the same way, or a run directory a driver is still writing, and prints, per cell, the arm, the implementer and route, the certificate, the attempts, the wall seconds, the steps, and the usage (a delegated cell's from its delegation records, as the runner reports it), then one line of totals per arm; the certificate counts, attempts, and usage the paragraphs below state are read from it. [`tools/build-dashboard.mjs`](tools/build-dashboard.mjs) folds every record and fold into [`dashboard.html`](dashboard.html), one self-contained page: the verdict of every paired comparison with its interval, the product models on sealed tier 5, the certification rate of every environment under every route, when each record ran, one row per record opening onto its cells and its paragraph here, the routing and repeatability readings, and one row per `bench loop` iteration once `loop/ledger.jsonl` exists; `--live <run dir>` adds a run a driver is still writing. [`improvement-log.md`](improvement-log.md) is the hand-written ledger over the same records and folds, one row per improvement iteration: the change proposed, what tested it, the paired reading, and the decision taken. [`tools/build-dataset.mjs`](tools/build-dataset.mjs) reads every record at once rather than one, folding their trajectories into a dataset under `datasets/<name>/` and refusing to write anything while any trajectory carries a credential- or mailbox-shaped string; `--purpose <delivery|training|evaluation>` keeps only the trajectories whose own `terms` admit that purpose and counts the rest as `with

## Running the bench

Run one fleet or one frozen experiment from a checked-in plan with the wrapper in `scripts/proving-ground.ts` (`pnpm run bench -- --help` lists every subcommand, `pnpm run bench -- plans` lists the checked-in plans). The route implementer is the operator's own Claude Code installation: log in with the `claude` CLI and have the product installed; no `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` is required.

```sh
pnpm run bench -- fleet h1-fleet-harness-loop-sonnet-t2
pnpm run bench -- experiment e3-attempts-t5
pnpm run bench -- loop nightly-tier5
pnpm run bench -- summarize <dir>
pnpm run bench -- record <dir> <name> --composition <composition path>
```

`loop <queue>` runs a checked-in queue rather than one plan. A queue under [`queues/`](../../examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/proving-ground-bench/queues/) is a JSON array of `{ plan, overlay, note }` entries — `overlay` is a name or `null` for the base composition, and `note` says why the entry is queued — resolved against the same plans and overlays as `fleet` and `experiment`, with an unknown name refused before the first driver starts. Each entry then runs in order: a `models` plan through the fleet driver and a `baseline`/`candidate` plan through the experiment driver, recorded as `<UTC date>-bench-<plan>` (suffixed `-2`, `-3`, … when that name is taken) by the same `record-run.mjs` a hand-recorded run uses, summarized, and written as one line of `loop/ledger.jsonl` carrying the verdict, delta, interval, and per-arm certificates read back out of that record. The decision rule is fixed and reads the verdict alone: `promote` decides `adopt-candidate`, `reject` and `inconclusive` decide `keep-baseline`, a fleet carries no verdict and decides `recorded`, and an entry whose driver or recording failed decides `none` and states its reason. A failed entry does not stop the queue; the command exits non-zero once it ends. `adopt-candidate` is a decision, not an edit: carrying a promoted arm into `cordis.yml` or an overlay is still a human act, as is the [improvement log](improvement-log.md) row that reads the ledger. `--dry-run` resolves everything and prints the schedule without running or writing anything, and `--from <n>` and `--only <plan>` resume a queue after an interruption. The schedule itself is outside the repository: an account Routine fires at 22:00 UTC into the operator's long-lived session — the checkout, the Claude Code login and the push access live there; a Routine created through the API carries no repository source, so a fresh session it spawns has neither a checkout nor push access, and the first two firings of that kind pushed nothing — and runs `git pull --rebase`, `node data/proving-ground/tools/preflight.mjs` (the install, the build, `claude --version`, `claude auth status`, `loop nightly-tier5 --dry-run`, and one line of `loop/preflight.jsonl` whether it passed or stopped), the loop, `build-dashboard.mjs`, a commit of `data/proving-ground/` alone per finished entry, a push; a preflight that stops commits and pushes its line and skips the loop, so a night that never reached the loop is on file with the step that stopped i

The same bench runs on an open-weight route through the `with-deepseek` overlay, which composes `@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm-deepseek` beside the base's product route: export `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` in the launching shell and add `--overlay with-deepseek` to a plan whose arms name `deepseek-official` (`h1-fleet-deepseek-t2` as a fleet, `e8-deepseek-vs-sonnet-t3` as a frozen pair against `sonnet`). Without that variable the fleet refuses the plan before its first cell and names the credential, so a keyless attempt costs nothing and reports why. This matters beyond portability: every record above was produced on the operator's Claude Code subscription, whose terms admit its transcripts as evaluation only, so none of this corpus may enter [the RLVR datasets](datasets/): `--purpose training` withholds every one of its trajectories, and a run on a route whose data-use terms allow training is the only kind it would not withhold. The `with-openrouter` overlay is that route: it composes `@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm-pi-ai` over OpenRouter's free tier with `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` exported in the launching shell, pins terms that admit training under their own agreement id, and its records of 2026-09-19 (the thirty-fourth and thirty-fifth above) are the first cells on another route: the first two launches certified none of their six cells, the loop's first iteration certified both of its two, and the agentic fleet certified 16 of 18 across three models. [`2026-09-19-openrouter-free-v1`](datasets/2026-09-19-openrouter-free-v1/README.md) is the first dataset built under `--purpose training`: 22 trajectories of the 852 the 35 exported records carry, 18 of them certified and 4 measured failures, on four free models over the six non-held-out tier-2 tasks; the two records exported before the fold wrote `terms` were re-exported for it by `tools/reexport-trajectories.mjs`, and the route's two partial records hold session logs and no export, so nothing in them is admitted.

1	# @deepseek-ai/dsh-tool-cordis
2	
3	English | [中文](README.zh.md)
4	
5	The self-referential Cordis toolset: five model-facing tools over the live runtime in the current DSH process. The registry, the vm sandbox, and the browser broadcast belong to [`@deepseek-ai/dsh-cordis-host-runner`](../cordis-host-runner/README.md) (`ctx.dynamic`), which this toolset injects — a composition with these tools but no runner never activates them. Design home — sandbox semantics, dynamic-package lifecycle and composition, standing decisions: [the toolset Agent Note](../../../.agents/notes/implemented/feature/2026-07-08-self-referential-cordis-toolset.md).
6	
7	`cordis_define`, `cordis_run`, `cordis_stop`, and `cordis_undefine` declare the `plugin-mount` tool authority because they mount or evaluate code in the live runtime; the three `cordis_inspect_*` tools declare `runtime-introspection` because they report the live composition. A composition that mounts a read barrier refuses either group in a session whose preset declares `role: implementer`, at the mount and again at execution; see [`dsh-read-barrier`](../../verification/read-barrier/README.md) for both refusals and their exact text.
8	
9	## What it does
10	
11	Two paired verbs, plus the read-only report.
12	
13	- `cordis_inspect` — read-only report over the current process: services, all live plugin fibers, registered tools, this session's dynamic packages, the reflection-backed `api` / `events` references, and the compile-time `client` slot surface a browser half can contribute UI into. An exact `name` with `what: "api"`, `what: "events"`, or `what: "client"` narrows the report and adds the full contract.
14	- `cordis_define` — records a package (`name`, `purpose`, and a host half `code` and/or a browser half `client`) after syntax-checking both halves. Nothing runs; the user sees a card for it in the conversation with a start control. The minted `dyn-<n>` id rides the result value AND the durable presentation metadata, which is how that card addresses the run verbs on replay.
15	- `cordis_run` — evaluates the host half in the sandbox and delivers the browser half to every open web page. Running an already-running package re-delivers the live version instead of failing, which is how a reloaded page gets it back.
16	- `cordis_stop` — disposes the host half to quiescence and withdraws the browser half; the definition survives and can run again.
17	- `cordis_undefine` — stops the package if needed and forgets the definition; its card stays in the conversation as an unloaded record.
18	
19	Exact model-facing schemas: [the generated tool catalog](../../../docs/tool-catalog.md).
20	
21	Dynamic packages live only in the shared DSH process memory. They remain active across later turns and may affect other sessions in that process, but disappear after `cordis_stop`/`cordis_undefine`, toolset unload, or DSH restart. They create no Plugin file, install no package, change no `cordis.yml` or personal/project configuration, do not survive restart, and cannot be promoted automatically. To keep an experiment, ask the Agent to implement a normal local, project, or repository Plugin through the regular development workflow. Every verb is session-scoped: a package is visible and controllable only in the session that defined it.
22	
23	## Trust stance
24	
25	The sandbox isolates globals but is not a security boundary. Node globals are absent or redirect to Cordis services such as `ctx.fs`, `ctx.web`, and `ctx.bash`, and writes to `globalThis` stay local, but host-realm helpers make escape possible. Mounted plugins receive a façade without framework internals, yet its allowed services affect the live runtime. Dynamic tool schemas and annotations cross the realm through iterative JSON cloning and schema normalization, so valid deep declarations are memory-bounded rather than call-stack-bounded; records with JSON-invisible keys and subclassed or decorated schema arrays reject before normalization. Treat this toolset like bash access; see the [design and trust stance](../../../.agents/notes/implemented/feature/2026-07-08-self-referential-cordis-toolset.md).
26	
27	## Config
28	
29	None. The vm evaluation bound (`vmTimeoutMs`) and the browser acknowledgement window (`ackTimeoutMs`) belong to the runner service that owns the sandbox and the broadcast — see [`@deepseek-ai/dsh-cordis-host-runner`](../cordis-host-runner/README.md#config).
30	
31	## The generated client slot catalog
32	
33	`src/client-catalog.ts` describes the browser half's seats, generated by `scripts/gen-client-catalog.ts` (freshness-gated by `pnpm run verify-client-catalog` in `doc-sync`) from a lexical scan of every `SlotMap` declaration merge and every `slots.register` call site. It carries the one surface a browser half can act on — the slot keys, each register call's options, the props a component receives, who already occupies the seat, and which owner's mount makes the seat exist — as plain data: this package stays host-side and imports no client module, so the strings are the only thing that crosses. The generator fails loud rather than shipping an entry a model cannot act on: a slot with no registrant-facing prose, a non-literal `kind`/`scope`, owner props no export provides, a duplicate key, or a registration into an undeclared slot all break the gate. Owner props expand one level — the owner declaration with its own member documentation, and the names of the shapes its fields reference — and one slot's whole report is budget-capped, because narrowing to a single slot exists to spend less context, not more.
34	
35	A slot's teaching text is its declaration's JSDoc, so improving what the model reads means editing the contract at its declaring package — not this catalog.
36	
37	## Where the API report comes from
38	
39	`cordis_inspect what:"api"` / `what:"events"` renders `src/api-catalog.ts`, the generated projection of the workspace's Cordis declarations: rendered method signatures, source JSDoc, harness events with their dispatch modes, and the type shapes those signatures reference, all produced by the same AST walk as `docs/subsystems`, so the data a model reads and the rendered docs cannot diverge. It is a compile-time fact about the REPOSITORY, so `pnpm run gen-cordis-api` regenerates it and `pnpm run verify-cordis-api` gates its freshness.
40	
41	`src/inspect.ts` intersects that catalog with the LIVE service store: what is RUNNING comes from the store, what each service CAN DO comes from the catalog, and a live service the catalog does not cover is reported as reachable with no signatures rather than omitted. A package that needs the list in its own code copies it out of a report — the catalog is a compile-time fact about the repository, so a copied list and a freshly read one say the same thing for any one deployment.
42	
43	Two model-facing judgements live in this package rather than in the artifacts, because reflection data is faithful to the code while a report has to be useful:
44	
45	- **Only callable methods are shown.** Non-method members are state rather than a verb, and their rendered form carries initializers from the implementation body; symbol-keyed members are internal seams between plugins that a package façade deliberately cannot reach, so naming one would advertise a call that cannot be made.
46	- **Only keys a host half can reach are named to a model.** The reflection model covers every `ctx.<key>` a package declares, including launcher-supplied boot values (`agent`, `headlessIo`, …) and browser-half services (`connection`). `src/curation.ts` classifies each one's `reach` — `injectable`, `not-a-service`, or `other-face` — and only `injectable` keys reach a report: naming a key a package cannot reach advertises a call that cannot be made. The classification is carried as data on each catalog entry rather than applied while rendering, so the exclusion is testable on its own, and `verify-cordis-catalog` pins the classified set to exactly the keys the documentation projection does not render — a newly declared key stops the gate instead of quietly inviting a model to `inject` something that will never arrive. A classified key that nonetheless has a live provider is still reported as running and injectable: the service store is the authority on what exists.
47	
48	The generated `INHERITED_CTX_API` closes the `api` report with the framework-inherited `ctx` surface (`ctx.on`, `ctx.effect`, `ctx.loader`, the timer helpers): those members are the Context itself rather than service keys, and the framework tier lives in pinned vendor packages outside every analyzed face, so the generator curates that one tier and renders it into both this catalog and `docs/cordis-api/inherited.md`. A live service the catalog does not describe is reported as running and still injectable rather than as absent. Broad `api` / `events` reports render summaries and signatures only; an exact `name` opts into the retained method/event JSDoc, and unknown or non-running service targets fail loud.
49	
50	## Rendering
51	
52	Every tool renders a `generic` card (`read` / `execute` / `delete`); `cordis_define` carries the submitted halves as `rawInput` and titles the card with the label and purpose. Presenters are pure functions of the args, and results keep the default text rendering. A Web client registers its own keyed `cordis_define` row (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-ui-cordis`) and reads the label, purpose, and minted id from the call arguments and the result metadata; the generic card is what a surface without that registration falls back to.
53	
54	## Export shape
55	
56	Namespace plugin: named exports `name` / `inject` / `apply`, no default export ([docs/postmortem/0001](../../../docs/postmortem/0001-acp-default-export-drops-inject.md)). It injects `tools` and `dynamicCordisRunner`.
57	
58	## Model Experience
59	
60	### Tool schemas
61	
62	#### What the model sees
63	
64	The conversation model sees the generated [`cordis_inspect`, `cordis_define`, `cordis_run`, `cordis_stop`, and `cordis_undefine` schemas](../../../docs/tool-catalog.md#deepseek-aidsh-tool-cordis) whenever this plugin is visible.
65	
66	#### Token effect
67	
68	Fixed schema cost on every request in that tool view.
69	
70	#### KV Cache effect
71	
72	Prefix-stable while this tool view is unchanged. Scoping or plugin lifecycle changes that hide these definitions may invalidate reuse from the first changed schema token.
73	
74	### Tool-call history and results
75	
76	#### What the model sees
77	
78	Inspect joins selected sections exactly as `## <section>` then a newline and the data-dependent body, with one blank line between sections; `what: "temporary"` uses the `## Dynamic Packages` heading. Each row reports the id, label, purpose, which halves exist, run state and revision, provided and awaited services, registered host methods, and the last browser-half load report. The empty state explains that definitions live only in this process's memory. Broad API/event reports omit JSDoc; `name` with `what: "api"`, `what: "events"`, or `what: "client"` returns one exact target with its full contract. The `client` section lists one seat per line with its cardinality, scope, summary, and whether registering there replaces shipped UI, then the cross-cutting registrant rules; the per-seat register options, owner and framework props, and runnable example arrive only under an exact `name`. Define answers that the package is defined and NOT running yet with the id to run; run reports the revision, what the host half provides or waits for, and whether a page acknowledged the browser half; stop and undefine acknowledge in one line. Every refusal is a tool error carrying the runner's teaching text. The submitted program remains in assistant tool-call history.
79	
80	#### Token effect
81	
82	Inspect output and submitted package code are data-dependent and resent until compaction; lifecycle acknowledgements are small. The `client` section is bounded by the shipped slot count (two lines each) and its per-seat detail is opt-in, so the default report grows with the slot surface rather than with its documentation.
83	
84	#### KV Cache effect
85	
86	Append-only; newly visible content follows the reusable request prefix and does not invalidate existing KV-cache entries.
87	
88	### Later requests after cordis_run
89	
90	#### What the model sees
91	
92	A running package may register tools, prompt contributions, or listeners that change later requests for the scopes it targets; `cordis_stop` and `cordis_undefine` remove those contributions after quiescence.
93	
94	#### Token effect
95	
96	Indirect token impact equals the running package's contributions and lasts only for its process-local lifetime.
97	
98	#### KV Cache effect
99	
100	Running or stopping a prompt or tool contribution changes later request prefixes and may invalidate reuse from the first changed contribution; an unchanged running set remains prefix-stable.
101	
102	## Known Limitations and Deferred Work
103	
104	- **The sandbox is containment for honest code, not a security boundary** — host-realm helpers on the sandbox global are reachable, so package code can reach Node; load this plugin as deliberately as you would grant a bash tool (see § Trust stance).
105	- **The `ctx` façade exposes no `effect()`** — package code cannot register a bespoke disposer; `on`/`provide`/`tools.register` are the supported cleanup paths.
106	- **The vm and acknowledgement bounds belong to the runner** — see its [Known Limitations](../cordis-host-runner/README.md#known-limitations-and-deferred-work); an async host-half body escapes `vmTimeoutMs`.

# Process transcripts

English | [中文](README.zh.md)

Complete transcripts of the agent sessions that build this repository, kept in the repository they build. Each build directory holds the raw Claude Code session tree as collected from the operator's machine and a compact dataset derived from it. They exist so that nothing about how this harness was made is lost: every prompt, tool call, and report is here to be mined for process patterns, failure taxonomies, and environment synthesis.

## Layout

```
data/transcripts/
  tools/
    collect-claude-code-session.mjs   snapshot one live Claude Code session into <build>/raw/
    transcripts-to-dataset.mjs        derive agents.jsonl, messages.jsonl, stats.json, and the README pair from a raw tree
  <date>-<label>/
    README.md, README.zh.md           generated provenance of that build: session id, repository head, counts
    agents.jsonl                      one record per transcript
    messages.jsonl                    one record per conversational message
    stats.json                        corpus totals and the subagent duration distribution
    raw/
      manifest.json                   session id, source directory, repository head, per-file bytes and SHA-256
      orchestrator-session.jsonl      the orchestrating session, as line-split parts above 40 MiB
      subagents/                      one JSONL transcript and one descriptor per background agent
      tool-results/                   tool output the session saved to disk when it overflowed a result
```

## Collecting a build

Run from the repository root inside the session being collected, or name the session and its project directory with `--session` and `--projects-dir`:

```sh
node data/transcripts/tools/collect-claude-code-session.mjs --out data/transcripts/2026-09-06-build/raw
node data/transcripts/tools/transcripts-to-dataset.mjs data/transcripts/2026-09-06-build/raw data/transcripts/2026-09-06-build
pnpm run verify-translation-pairing --write data/transcripts/2026-09-06-build/README.md
```

The collector refuses to write while any credential-shaped string in the sources lacks an `--accept-hit <sha256>` naming the reviewed match; a refused run prints every match with the flag to pass, and the accepted digests are recorded in `manifest.json`. It splits files above 40 MiB at line boundaries so no blob exceeds GitHub's per-file ceiling, records every file's digest, and leaves an unchanged tree untouched, so it runs repeatedly during a build without churn. Commit the raw tree, the regenerated dataset, and the re-recorded pairing together.

## What the data is and is not

- The raw tree is verbatim: message text, tool inputs, tool results, token usage, and timing as Claude Code logged them, including the operator's account e-mail where the harness's context reminders carried it. Credential-shaped strings are refused, never rewritten.

30:The registry is process memory and the only source of truth. The session log carries a define call's metadata — never its code — so a restarted process legitimately has no definitions, and a card whose id no longer resolves says exactly that rather than pretending it can run. Nothing here is written to disk, and no definition is restored automatically; a reloaded page holds nothing until someone runs a package again, which is what makes it bind the live host half and re-fetch the browser half.

1	# Code-safety runs
2	
3	English | [中文](README.zh.md)
4	
5	Records of real code-safety reviews: one program per record, kept exactly as the harness released it. A record holds the report the program published, the union of findings behind it, the verdict the committed examiner gave over the merged head, every session log, and a manifest with the repository head, the composition, the locked target and every file's digest. Nothing in a record is edited after the run; the table below is read from those files. One thing is changed before a record is committed: private key material and example cloud keys that a department read out of the target are replaced in the findings, the result and the session logs by a redaction marker, and `manifest.json` lists under `redactions` which files were touched and how many blocks; the lines the examiner verified are never among them.
6	
7	The program is [`examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/program-code-safety/`](../../examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/program-code-safety/README.md), which also documents what a finding has to be and what the examiner refuses.
8	
9	## Layout
10	
11	```
12	data/code-safety/
13	  <date>-<target>/
14	    manifest.json      repository head, composition, locked target, per-department outcome, findings per severity and confidence, per-file bytes and SHA-256
15	    result.json        the driver's result line: the ledger, the member sessions, the barrier refusals, the released file list
16	    SAFETY-REPORT.md   the report the program released, verbatim
17	    findings.json      the union of every department's findings, as released
18	    verifier.txt       the committed examiner's exit code and output over the released worktree
19	    stderr.txt         what the driver wrote to stderr, when it wrote anything
20	    sessions/          every session log: the ledger, the six departments and the integration, named by session id
21	  targets/<target>.ground-truth.json   a target's own documented defects, for reading a record's recall against; never part of the release gate
22	  tools/record-run.mjs                 copies one run directory into a record and writes its manifest
23	  tools/recall.mjs                     reads a record's recall against a ground-truth list; never part of the release gate
24	  tools/compare.mjs                    scores any findings list against a ground truth, the rule recall.mjs uses, for a cross-tool comparison
25	  tools/trajectory.mjs                 reads a record's session logs for its provenance and each finding's read trail
26	  tools/assemble-comparison.mjs        assembles one target's three-tier comparison into comparisons/<date>-<target>/comparison.json
27	  comparisons/<date>-<target>/         a target reviewed three ways — a scanner, one model, the enterprise — scored against one ground truth
28	```
29	
30	## Running one, and recording it
31	
32	```sh
33	pnpm run code-safety -- /path/to/target --out .code-safety/<name> --model sonnet
34	node data/code-safety/tools/record-run.mjs .code-safety/<name> <date>-<target> \
35	  --composition examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/program-code-safety/overlays/claude-code.cordis.yml
36	```
37	
38	The recorder refuses to overwrite an existing record. Add a row below afterwards, and keep whatever the run exposed — a department that ran out of rounds, an integration that never passed the examiner — beside it rather than rerunning until it looks clean.
39	
40	## Runs
41	
42	| Run | Head | Target | Model | Certified | Findings | Examiner | Elapsed |
43	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
44	| [2026-09-19-nodegoat](2026-09-19-nodegoat/manifest.json) | `be507df30` | OWASP NodeGoat, 111 files | `sonnet` | 7 of 7 | 42 (5 critical, 17 high, 13 medium, 5 low, 2 info) | exit 0 | 1301 s |
45	| [2026-09-19-dvja](2026-09-19-dvja/manifest.json) | `3d386bac2` | dvja (Java, Struts 2 and Spring), 174 files | `sonnet` | 7 of 7 | 40 (9 critical, 10 high, 13 medium, 7 low, 1 info) | exit 0 | 1414 s |
46	| [2026-09-19-nodegoat-2](2026-09-19-nodegoat-2/manifest.json) | `5a59895fa` | OWASP NodeGoat, 111 files, started through the feed's `POST /safety` | `sonnet` | 7 of 7 | 38 (4 critical, 16 high, 14 medium, 4 low) | exit 0 | 1225 s |
47	| [2026-09-21-nodegoat-3](2026-09-21-nodegoat-3/manifest.json) | `a47c8f519` | OWASP NodeGoat, 111 files, started through the hosted mirror relay's `POST /safety` | `sonnet` | 7 of 7 | 47 (4 critical, 18 high, 17 medium, 7 low, 1 info) | exit 0 | 1356 s |
48	
49	## What a record proves
50	
51	That every finding in `findings.json` existed at the line it cites, in the tree `manifest.json` locks, at the moment the examiner ran; that the report's own counts are the union's; and that nothing a department reported was dropped without being named. It does not prove that a listed finding is exploitable, that an unlisted defect is absent, or that the review read any file it does not say it read. `## Scope and method` and `## What was not covered` in each report are the bounds, and they are part of the record for that reason.
52	
53	A record's recall against a target's documented defects is a separate reading, taken from `targets/<target>.ground-truth.json` beside the record rather than inside the release gate: a gate that scored recall could only run on targets whose defects are already known, which is not the case this program exists for. `node data/code-safety/tools/recall.mjs <record> <ground truth>` prints that reading: a known issue counts as found when a released finding cites its file within three lines of its range or one of the other locations the ground truth lists for the same defect. On the NodeGoat record it reads 14 of 18: the four the review missed are the log injection on the login path, the distinct error messages that enumerate users, the one-character password policy, and the catastrophic regular expression on the routing number, and 12 of the 42 released findings are defects the ground truth does not list, among them the hard-coded administrator password the reset script seeds, the private key committed under `artifacts/`, the session that is not regenerated at login, and the dependency advisories read from the lockfile. The dvja record (a Java Struts 2 application, 174 files, reviewed before the departments were told to run semgrep first) reads 13 of 14: the one issue the review missed is the profile update that trusts a caller-supplied user id, and 14 of its 40 findings are beyond the list, among them the Log4Shell-era log4j, the cookie-gated bulk export of every user's personal data, and the root password committed in the compose file.
54	
55	Two reviews of the same NodeGoat revision on the same composition, three hours apart, are the repeatability reading: the second released 38 findings to the first's 42; 38 of the first's 42 have a second-run finding within three lines of the same file, 31 of them with the same CWE, and 33 of the second's 38 have a first-run match; both read 14 of 18 with the same four misses, and they cite 15 files in common. The runs differ in the low-severity tail and in how one defect is split into findings, not in the certified core. A third NodeGoat review on 2026-09-21, on the same composition and started through the hosted mirror relay, released 47 findings and reads 13 of 18; its misses are on the session (three), research and profile routes.
56

1	#!/usr/bin/env node
2	// Reads a code-safety record's session logs and emits two things the raw
3	// findings do not carry: the trajectory behind each finding (which department
4	// agent read the finding's file, over how many steps and tool calls, before it
5	// reported), and the record's provenance (how much work the agents did on their
6	// own against how many times a human acted). Both come from the committed
7	// session logs, so the record proves who did the work rather than asserting it.
8	//
9	// A department session file is named `program-<hash>-<dept>.jsonl`; the lead is
10	// `program-<hash>.jsonl` and the integration `...-~0040integration.jsonl`
11	// (`~0040` is the encoded `@`). A finding is attributed to its department by an
12	// explicit `department` field or by its id prefix (`injection-...`), the same
13	// rule the feed uses. A read counts as touching a finding's file when the read
14	// target path ends with the finding's repo-relative file.
15	//
16	// Usage: node trajectory.mjs <record dir> [--json]
17	import { readFileSync, readdirSync } from 'node:fs'
18	import { join } from 'node:path'
19	
20	const [recordDir, ...flags] = process.argv.slice(2)
21	if (!recordDir) {
22	  console.error('usage: node trajectory.mjs <record dir> [--json]')
23	  process.exit(2)
24	}
25	const asJson = flags.includes('--json')
26	
27	const findings = (() => {
28	  const raw = JSON.parse(readFileSync(join(recordDir, 'findings.json'), 'utf8'))
29	  return Array.isArray(raw) ? raw : raw.findings ?? []
30	})()
31	
32	const sessionsDir = join(recordDir, 'sessions')
33	const files = readdirSync(sessionsDir).filter(name => name.endsWith('.jsonl'))
34	
35	/** The department a session file names: `-injection` → injection, the encoded `-~0040integration` → integration, the bare lead file → lead. */
36	function departmentOf(name) {
37	  const match = /^program-[0-9a-f]+(?:-(.+))?\.jsonl$/.exec(name)
38	  const suffix = match?.[1]
39	  if (suffix === undefined) return 'lead'
40	  return suffix.replaceAll(/~([0-9a-f]{4})/g, (_, hex) => String.fromCharCode(Number.parseInt(hex, 16))).replace(/^@/, '')
41	}
42	
43	/** Parse a session file into the facts the digest needs: steps, tool calls by name, files read, human turns, whether it certified. */
44	function foldSession(path) {
45	  const lines = readFileSync(path, 'utf8').trim().split('\n')
46	  const tools = {}
47	  const filesRead = new Set()
48	  let steps = 0
49	  let certified = false
50	  for (const line of lines) {
51	    let event
52	    try {
53	      event = JSON.parse(line)
54	    } catch {
55	      continue
56	    }
57	    const type = event.type
58	    if (type === 'step/start') steps += 1
59	    else if (type === 'verification/certificate') certified = true
60	    else if (type === 'tool/call') {
61	      const name = event.data?.name ?? 'tool'
62	      tools[name] = (tools[name] ?? 0) + 1
63	      if (name === 'read') {
64	        try {
65	          const path = JSON.parse(event.data?.arguments ?? '{}').file_path
66	          if (typeof path === 'string') filesRead.add(path)
67	        } catch {
68	          // A read whose arguments did not parse contributes no file, not an error.
69	        }
70	      }
71	    }
72	  }
73	  const toolCalls = Object.values(tools).reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0)
74	  return { steps, toolCalls, tools, filesRead: [...filesRead], certified }
75	}
76	
77	const departments = files
78	  .map(name => ({ name, department: departmentOf(name), ...foldSession(join(sessionsDir, name)) }))
79	  .sort((a, b) => a.department.localeCompare(b.department))
80	
81	/** The department a finding belongs to: its explicit field, else its id prefix. */
82	function findingDepartment(finding) {
83	  if (typeof finding.department === 'string') return finding.department
84	  const id = typeof finding.id === 'string' ? finding.id : ''
85	  const known = departments.map(d => d.department).filter(d => d !== 'lead' && d !== 'integration')
86	  return known.find(d => id.startsWith(`${d}-`)) ?? 'unknown'
87	}
88	
89	const readsByDepartment = new Map(departments.map(d => [d.department, d.filesRead]))
90	const trajectories = findings.map(finding => {
91	  const department = findingDepartment(finding)
92	  const reads = readsByDepartment.get(department) ?? []
93	  const readItsFile = typeof finding.file === 'string' && reads.some(path => path.endsWith(`/${finding.file}`) || path.endsWith(finding.file))
94	  return { id: finding.id, department, file: finding.file, line: finding.line, severity: finding.severity, readItsFile }
95	})
96	
97	const agentSessions = departments.filter(d => d.steps > 0)
98	const provenance = {
99	  // One operator command starts the program; the lead fans it out to the
100	  // departments and the integration, so every session below the lead is an
101	  // agent the run created, not a person. This count is the record's own fact.
102	  operatorCommands: 1,
103	  agentSessions: agentSessions.length,
104	  autonomousSteps: departments.reduce((sum, d) => sum + d.steps, 0),
105	  autonomousToolCalls: departments.reduce((sum, d) => sum + d.toolCalls, 0),
106	  departmentsCertified: departments.filter(d => d.certified).length,
107	  findingsWithReadTrail: trajectories.filter(t => t.readItsFile).length,
108	  findings: trajectories.length,
109	}
110	
111	const digest = {
112	  record: recordDir.split('/').pop(),
113	  provenance,
114	  departments: departments.map(({ name: _name, filesRead, ...rest }) => ({ ...rest, filesRead: filesRead.length })),
115	  trajectories,
116	}
117	
118	if (asJson) {
119	  console.log(JSON.stringify(digest, null, 2))
120	} else {
121	  console.log(`record ${digest.record}`)
122	  console.log(`provenance: ${provenance.agentSessions} agent sessions, ${provenance.autonomousSteps} steps, ${provenance.autonomousToolCalls} tool calls, ${provenance.departmentsCertified} certified; ${provenance.findingsWithReadTrail}/${provenance.findings} findings on a file their department read`)
123	  for (const d of departments) console.log(`  ${d.department.padEnd(13)} ${String(d.steps).padStart(3)} steps ${String(d.toolCalls).padStart(3)} tools ${String(d.filesRead.length).padStart(3)} files read${d.certified ? ' certified' : ''}`)
124	}

     1	#!/usr/bin/env node
     2	// Scores one tier of a code-safety comparison against a target's ground truth,
     3	// using the same match rule as recall.mjs: a known issue counts as found when a
     4	// finding cites the issue's file within three lines of its range or one of its
     5	// `alsoAt` locations. A tier is a plain findings list (id, file, line,
     6	// severity, cwe, title) from any producer — a scanner, a single model, or the
     7	// enterprise program — normalized to that schema before it reaches here, so
     8	// every tier is scored identically. Recall is against the 18 known issues;
     9	// precision here is the share of a tier's findings that land on a known issue,
    10	// a floor on real precision because a finding beyond the ground truth may still
    11	// be real (the list is not exhaustive), which the report states.
    12	//
    13	// Usage: node compare.mjs <findings json> <ground-truth json> [--json]
    14	import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs'
    15	
    16	const [findingsPath, groundTruthPath, ...flags] = process.argv.slice(2)
    17	if (!findingsPath || !groundTruthPath) {
    18	  console.error('usage: node compare.mjs <findings json> <ground-truth json> [--json]')
    19	  process.exit(2)
    20	}
    21	const asJson = flags.includes('--json')
    22	const raw = JSON.parse(readFileSync(findingsPath, 'utf8'))
    23	const findings = Array.isArray(raw) ? raw : raw.findings ?? []
    24	const truth = JSON.parse(readFileSync(groundTruthPath, 'utf8'))
    25	const TOLERANCE = 3
    26	
    27	const within = (finding, file, lines) => finding.file === file && typeof finding.line === 'number' && finding.line >= lines[0] - TOLERANCE && finding.line <= lines[1] + TOLERANCE
    28	const rows = truth.issues.map(issue => {
    29	  const locations = [{ file: issue.file, lines: issue.lines }, ...(issue.alsoAt ?? [])]
    30	  const matched = findings.filter(f => locations.some(l => within(f, l.file, l.lines)))
    31	  return { id: issue.id, category: issue.category, file: `${issue.file}:${issue.lines.join('-')}`, found: matched.length > 0 }
    32	})
    33	const found = rows.filter(r => r.found).length
    34	// A finding lands on a known issue when it matches any issue's location.
    35	const onKnown = findings.filter(f => truth.issues.some(issue => [{ file: issue.file, lines: issue.lines }, ...(issue.alsoAt ?? [])].some(l => within(f, l.file, l.lines)))).length
    36	const summary = {
    37	  target: truth.target,
    38	  revision: truth.revision,
    39	  knownIssues: rows.length,
    40	  found,
    41	  recall: Number((found / rows.length).toFixed(3)),
    42	  findings: findings.length,
    43	  onKnownIssue: onKnown,
    44	  precisionOnKnown: findings.length > 0 ? Number((onKnown / findings.length).toFixed(3)) : 0,
    45	  beyondGroundTruth: findings.length - onKnown,
    46	}
    47	
    48	if (asJson) {
    49	  console.log(JSON.stringify({ ...summary, rows }, null, 2))
    50	} else {
    51	  for (const r of rows) console.log(`${r.found ? 'found ' : 'missed'}  ${r.id.padEnd(9)} ${r.file}`)
    52	  console.log(`recall ${found}/${rows.length} (${summary.recall}) on ${truth.target} at ${truth.revision.slice(0, 7)}; ${findings.length} findings, ${onKnown} on a known issue, ${summary.beyondGroundTruth} beyond`)
    53	}

1	# Agent Note: Where the four objectives stand, what blocks each, and the order of work
2	
3	Status: proposed
4	
5	English | [中文](2026-09-19-objectives-step-back.zh.md)
6	
7	## Problem
8	
9	The project has four objectives: a harness that makes any model the best agentic coder it can be, agentic software creation through that harness, a roughly 120B open-weight model trained by RLVR on the harness's certified runs, and a loop in which the harness improves itself by evidence. Two weeks of building produced the instrument (a 40-environment bench with validator-held cases, sealed cells, frozen paired experiments with bootstrap verdicts, a runner with attempt ladders and budget shares, a program workflow, a trajectory exporter and dataset builder, terms gating, a dashboard) and 32 recorded runs, 920 cells, and 844 certificates ([data/proving-ground](../../../../data/proving-ground/README.md)). What nobody has written down is how far each objective actually is from "partly done", which facts block it, and what order the remaining work should take. Without that, effort keeps flowing to whatever is nearest.
10	
11	## Proposal
12	
13	State the standing of each objective from the records, name the blocker, and take the work in the order below.
14	
15	### Objective 1: the best harness for any model
16	
17	Standing: the instrument exists and discriminates at tier 5 only; the harness has not yet shown a certificate win over the product's own loop, and every one of the 32 records ran one provider's models through the operator's Claude Code login. The paired readings in [the results note](../architecture/2026-09-08-hypothesis-program-results.md) are: the harness loop equals the product loop on certificates at tiers 3 and 5 (0 and −0.0625, both inside the one-flip noise floor) while being faster in 15 of 16 sealed pairs and 3.4 times cheaper in billed tokens; the largest model certifies every sealed tier-5 cell; attempts matter (three against one, +0.375); knowledge packs, craft skills, model cascades, and a dropped transcript add no certificates, and the cascade with a bounded cheap rung (E6) recovers the certificates the unbounded one lost at twice the cost. The bench below tier 5 is saturated by every model, and tier 5 is saturated by the largest one.
18	
19	Blockers: one provider; a top tier the largest model saturates; a noise floor of one to two flips at sixteen pairs.
20	
21	Next: run the bench on a second model family the moment a key exists (the open-weight overlay below); add a tier the largest model does not saturate (multi-file tasks with a repository and a spec, hidden cases held by the validator, the same admission and fairness audit as tier 5); test mechanisms with a stated hypothesis of effect on the middle model at tier 5, one per frozen pair (E7, five attempts against three, is running; then a self-review rung before validation and a directive that carries the validator's channel diff); run two seeds per experiment so a reading has thirty-two pairs.
22	
23	### Objective 2: agentic software creation through the harness
24	
25	Standing: the program workflow (departments in worktrees, integration, committed verifier, commit-or-refuse) has run once for real, producing an assessment document, never a piece of software.
26	
27	Next: the `csv-tools` program (three departments, a spec, a `node:test` verifier) prepared today and run on the route after E7; then a program that builds a plugin for this repository under its own gates, which is the dogfooding case the objective actually means.
28	
29	### Objective 3: the open-weight model trained by RLVR
30	
31	Standing: the pipeline exists and was exercised as a dry run: 750 trajectories in the `dsh-trajectory/1` format, 521 on the harness route, in [the v1 dataset fold](../../../../data/proving-ground/datasets/2026-09-18-proving-ground-v1/README.md), with rewards from certificates and parity. Not one of them may train the Daliesk model: all ran on the operator's Claude Code login, and the [data-use terms](../../../../packages/governance/data-use/README.md) admit into the training corpus only sessions pinned with terms that allow it, which only a route on an open-weight model can carry. The corpus that matters is therefore empty, and no training compute is attached to this repository.
32	
33	Blockers, in order: a key for an open-weight route (`DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` for [`dsh-llm-deepseek`](../../../../packages/llm/llm-deepseek/README.md), or a gateway key through [`dsh-llm-pi-ai`](../../../../packages/llm/llm-pi-ai/README.md)); the base-model decision, still open; compute for the RLVR run itself.
34	
35	Next, without a key: the `with-deepseek` and gateway overlays with their plans, so the bench runs on an open model one environment variable after the key arrives, and the corpus fills from those runs alone; the training recipe as a proposed note (certified trajectories as the SFT warm-up, the validator as the RLVR reward over the same environments, held-out environments as the only reported number). With a key: the tier-2 fleet first, then the tier-3 frozen pair against the middle product model, recorded like every other run.
36	
37	### Objective 4: the self-improvement loop
38	
39	Standing: every piece exists and has run (frozen pairs, the verdict rule, composition manifests, the program workflow), but each iteration was proposed by a person, launched by hand through `pnpm run bench`, and applied by editing a composition. The iterations are legible only across a note, thirty-two records, and ten folds.
40	
41	Next: the improvement log under `data/proving-ground/` as the ledger of every iteration with its verdict and decision (today), then the propose step inside the harness (a department reads the ledger and the bench's misses and writes a candidate overlay and plan), scheduled launches through the shift driver, and promotion through the composition manifest rather than a hand edit.
42	
43	### Order of work
44	
45	Today: E7 recorded; the open-weight overlays, plans, and keyless refusal; the improvement log; the `csv-tools` program run and recorded; the dashboard and this note updated. Next: the tier above tier 5; the self-review rung as a frozen pair; the propose step. Needed from the operator: a key for an open-weight route in the environment, a decision on training compute, and the base model.
46	
47	## Alternatives considered
48	
49	- Keep running experiments on the one provider until an effect appears. Rejected: the top tier is saturated by the largest model, and no trajectory from that provider can train the model, so the runs would answer neither objective 1 nor 3.
50	- Build the next bench tier before the open-weight route. Deferred: the tier matters most once a second model family runs, and the route is one variable away while the tier is days of authoring and audit.
51	- Call the harness state of the art now. Rejected: on the recorded evidence it equals the product loop on certificates, on one provider, and is cheaper; that is a cost result, not a capability result.
52	
53	## Acceptance criteria
54	
55	- One run on an open-weight route recorded under `data/proving-ground/` with terms that admit training, and the corpus fold counting at least one admitted trajectory.
56	- The `csv-tools` program certified by its verifier and recorded as a program record.
57	- The improvement log carrying E7's verdict and decision.
58	- The next bench tier admitted with the fairness audit, and one frozen pair on it.
59	
60	## Risks
61	
62	- The shared subscription's rate limits and the container's restarts (two on 2026-09-18) can cut a run; the partial-record path keeps what ran.
63	- Sixteen-pair readings invite over-reading; the note's noise-floor rule stands.
64	- A dataset that mixes provider-of-record trajectories into training would breach the terms; the curator withholds them, and the fold's manifest names every source record so a reader can check.
65

1	# Agent Note: The bench loop and its machine ledger
2	
3	Status: implemented
4	
5	English | [中文](2026-09-19-bench-loop-and-machine-ledger.zh.md)
6	
7	## Problem
8	
9	[The improvement log](../../../../data/proving-ground/improvement-log.md) listed four parts of the improvement loop that a person supplies. Two of them were mechanical work rather than judgment: a run was launched one plan at a time, and the reading it produced was copied into the log by hand. Launching one plan at a time meant an operator sat through each run to start the next, so a night's worth of comparisons needed a night's worth of attention, and nothing recorded what had been queued or why. Copying the reading by hand meant the log's numbers were a transcription of `result.json`, with no file between the record and the row that any later reader could replay: an iteration that ran but never gained a row left no trace of its verdict outside the record directory, and a row's numbers could drift from the record without any gate noticing.
10	
11	## Decision
12	
13	`pnpm run bench -- loop <queue>` runs an ordered queue of checked-in plans unattended. A queue is JSON — a checked-in name under [`queues/`](../../../../examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/proving-ground-bench/queues/) or a path — holding an array of `{ plan, overlay, note }` entries: `overlay` is an overlay name or `null` for the fixture's base composition, and `note` says why the entry is queued. `nightly-tier5.json` is the checked-in example. Every entry resolves through the same `resolvePlanPath` and `resolveOverlayPath` the `fleet` and `experiment` subcommands use, and the whole queue resolves before the first driver starts, so an unknown plan or overlay anywhere in the file refuses the command rather than stopping it halfway. An entry's driver follows from the plan itself: a `models` array is a fleet, a `baseline`/`candidate` pair is an experiment, and a plan declaring both or neither is refused.
14	
15	Each entry runs into a run directory under the wrapper's runs root, exactly as `fleet` and `experiment` do, then is recorded by the same `record-run.mjs` a hand-recorded run uses, under `<UTC date>-bench-<plan>` with `-2`, `-3`, … appended when that name is taken, then summarized, then written as one line of `data/proving-ground/loop/ledger.jsonl`. The line carries `ranAt`, `queue`, `index`, `plan`, `overlay`, `kind`, `record`, `head`, `verdict`, `delta`, `interval`, `certified` per arm, `decision`, `elapsedSeconds`, `outcome`, and `reason` on a failure. Every number on it is read back out of the record that was just written — an experiment's verdict, delta, and interval from its `result.json`, each arm's certificates from that result's per-environment rates and pair counts, a fleet's certificates per model from its leaderboard, the elapsed seconds from the manifest — so the ledger states what the record states and invents nothing.
16	
17	The decision rule is fixed in code and documented with it: verdict `promote` decides `adopt-candidate`, `reject` and `inconclusive` decide `keep-baseline`, a fleet carries no verdict and decides `recorded`, and a failed entry decides `none`. `adopt-candidate` names a decision, not an edit. Nothing in the loop writes a composition, because an arm cannot name one: carrying a promoted arm into `cordis.yml` or an overlay stays the human act the improvement log's third limitation describes.
18	
19	A failed entry — a driver that exited non-zero, a recording `record-run.mjs` refused, a record whose result carries neither a verdict nor a leaderboard — is written to the ledger as `outcome: "failed"` with its reason, and the queue continues to the next entry; the command exits non-zero once the queue ends. `--dry-run` resolves everything, prints the schedule, and runs and writes nothing. `--from <n>` and `--only <plan>` resume a queue after an interruption, and both narrow the resolved queue rather than the parsed one, so a typo in a skipped entry is still refused.
20	
21	The ledger is machine-owned and append-only: the loop writes it, nothing else does, and it is absent until the first iteration runs. [`build-dashboard.mjs`](../../../../data/proving-ground/tools/build-dashboard.mjs) reads it when it exists and renders a Loop section — when, queue and position, plan, overlay, kind, per-arm certificates, delta with interval, verdict, decision, wall time, and a link to the record — which stays hidden while the ledger is absent or empty, like the page's Running-now section. The records' own lanes, cards, and rows are untouched. [The improvement log](../../../../data/proving-ground/improvement-log.md) remains hand-written and remains the ledger a reader reads; what changed is that its rows now read a durable, replayable machine line instead of a record directory alone.
22	
23	## Alternatives considered
24	
25	- **Generate the improvement log's rows from the ledger.** Rejected for the same reason [the improvement-log note](2026-09-19-improvement-log-as-the-loop-ledger.md) rejected generating them from the records: the proposed change, the reason a decision was taken, and the default that moved are in no file the loop writes. The ledger carries a decision label, not the sentence that weighs a verdict against its cost, and generating the two columns a machine can fill would leave the log's actual subject in a hand-maintained sidecar.
26	- **Extend the improvement log itself with machine-appended rows.** Rejected: a Markdown table that both a person and a command write has no owner, and a machine append would conflict with the editorial rewriting a row's decision column needs. Keeping the machine ledger in its own JSONL file gives each artifact one writer and makes the machine's half diffable line by line.
27	- **Let the loop apply an adopted candidate to the composition.** Rejected: an experiment arm names a route and a ladder, not a composition, so there is no mechanical translation from a promoted arm to a `cordis.yml` edit, and a verdict on sixteen cells is not by itself a reason to move a shipped default. The rule names the decision and stops there.
28	- **Stop the queue at the first failure.** Rejected: the failures worth surviving are per-run — a driver that died on one plan, a container restart, a record name already taken — and the remaining entries are independent runs. Stopping would forfeit a night of runs to one bad entry; the non-zero exit at the end keeps the failure visible.
29	- **Schedule the queue as well, with cron or a verdict trigger.** Deferred: a schedule needs a policy for what to queue and when to stop, and the bench runs on the operator's own subscription. The loop closes the launching gap; an account Routine enabled by the operator fires at 22:00 UTC into the operator's long-lived session, where the checkout, the Claude Code login and the push access live (a Routine created through the API carries no repository source, so the fresh sessions its first version spawned had neither a checkout nor push access and pushed nothing), runs the instructions the [records README](../../../../data/proving-ground/README.md) lists, and records its preflight — install, build, CLI, login, dry run — as one line of `loop/preflight.jsonl` through [`preflight.mjs`](../../../../data/proving-ground/tools/preflight.mjs), pushing that line even when it stops there; the improvement log still records that no verdict-driven trigger exists.
30	
31	## Consequences
32	
33	- One command runs a night of comparisons: a queue of three tier-5 plans records three runs, decides three times, and leaves three ledger lines, where an operator previously started each run and read each result.
34	- The machine's half of the loop is replayable. Every ledger line names its record, its head, and its queue position, so a row of the improvement log can be checked against the record it claims to read, and an iteration that never gained a row is still on file.
35	- The ledger is a new durable format with no compatibility promise, in line with the pre-release stance: it is append-only JSONL, read by `build-dashboard.mjs` and by people, and a field added to the line changes the page's Loop section in the same change.
36	- Failure states are recorded rather than lost: a driver that exits non-zero leaves a line naming its run directory, and a record the reading cannot interpret leaves a line naming the record.
37	- A firing that never reaches the loop is recorded too: `loop/preflight.jsonl` gains one line per firing, passed or stopped, and the stopping step's exit status and last output name what the environment lacked.
38	- `scripts/proving-ground.spec.ts` covers queue parsing and its refusals, plan and overlay resolution, plan classification, record-name suffixing, the decision rule, the reading of two checked-in records, the ledger line, and the end-to-end `--dry-run` over the checked-in queue. A real queued run needs the operator's Claude Code subscription, so no test runs a driver.
39

### W4 — Fleet observatory and two-speed improvement

Goal 4 — the loop that feeds both the harness and the model. A fast loop where agents write and refine skills in their department layer under a deterministic keep-or-retire scoreboard, and a slow loop where frozen experiments and attributable humans move knowledge into the fleet. Both read one content-addressed ledger; the observatory is a projection of the log, not a pipeline beside it.

| Stage | Actor | Type | Status | Emits | Plugins | On failure |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Manifest and facts | Scorekeeper | STORE | partial | `CompositionManifest`, `ScoreboardBatch` | existing: trajectories, session-projection, scorekeeper (the `sessionFacts` projection); new: components-manifest plugin, skill digests | A skill result whose digest is not in the manifest fails the invariant. |
| 2. Scoreboards and alerts | Scorekeeper | D | partial | `Alert` | existing: scorekeeper, budget-policy, experiments (the statistics); new: alert thresholds | A metric without enough sessions is not alerted on. |
| 3. Diagnosis | Trajectory Analyst (cross-model) | DS | proposed | `SessionDiagnosis` | existing: session-query, subagent `outputSchema`; new: trajectory-analyst preset | A diagnosis never retires an environment or sets a budget; it opens a dispute or a proposal. |
| 4. Fast tier: session and department skills | Department agents | S | partial | `KnowledgeProposal` | existing: layered `ctx.skills`, agent-presets layers; new: `dsh-skill-synthesized` provider, tenant scope on skills | A candidate without evidence sessions or scope is rejected by schema. |
| 5. Keep or retire | Department scoreboard | D | proposed | `ScoreboardBatch` | existing: scorekeeper, experiments; new: presets as an arm dimension, paired present-versus-absent cells | A skill without paired runs is neither kept nor retired; it stays tier 0. |
| 6. Nomination and frozen experiment | Experiment service | D | partial | `ExperimentPlan`, `ExperimentResult` | existing: schedule, environment-runner, experiments (the plan digest, the paired run, the budget refusal); new: nomination, cells derived by rule | A plan over budget waits; a plan above the cap needs a human. |
| 7. Static gates | run-gates | GATE | partial | `GateReport` | existing: scripts/run-gates | Findings return to stage 4. |
| 8. Promotion | Attributed human signer (maintainer) | HUMAN | partial | `PromotionDecision`, `SignoffRecord` | existing: .agents/notes process, approval seam; new: `signoff/recorded` event | A rejection stays in the ledger with its reason. |
| 9. Knowledge ledger | Archive sampler | STORE | proposed | `HarnessVariant` | existing: storage, components; new: `dsh-archive` | A ledger entry with no matching manifest occurrence never counts as having been in play. |
| 10. Data steering | Data Curator | D | proposed | `CurriculumUpdate` | new: curator plugin | — feeds W3's calibration. |
| 11. Audit | Scorekeeper | STORE | proposed | `AuditReport` | existing: session-persistence; new: tamper evidence and erasure in persistence, oversight-seam monitor | — |

The fast tier (stage 4) lets an agent write a skill after use and refine it by re-registration inside its own department layer — nothing here is fleet-shared, model-visible outside that layer, or exported — and only a candidate with evidence sessions and a declared scope of session, department, or client is eligible for the deterministic keep-or-retire scoreboard (stage 5), which compares paired present-versus-absent cells and marks a skill deprecated once its delta stays at or below zero over the configured number of runs.

The slow tier freezes a nominated proposal's digest before any cell runs (stage 6), derives cells from the diagnosis evidence plus a stratified held-in sample plus a held-out regression by a logged deterministic rule, and never lets an S field set priority; prompt sections, tool schemas, and skills always need a human at promotion (stage 8), while policy and presentation changes with no model-visible text may promote on the experiment alone.

The knowledge ledger (stage 9) keeps every `id@digest` with lineage, evidence sessions, results, and decisions, losers included, mirrored against the composition manifest so replay can tell exactly which components were in play; audit (stage 11) hash-chains persisted artefacts per checkpoint and signs daily manifests to write-once storage, with a per-client crypto-shredding key for erasure.

### W4

- A `CompositionManifest` event names every component in play as `id@digest` at session start and on every preset, skill, or tool-set change, and an invariant rejects a skill result whose digest is absent from the manifest.
- A tier-1 skill candidate carries evidence sessions and a declared scope of session, department, or client, or is rejected by schema; the department scoreboard marks a skill deprecated only after paired present-versus-absent runs show a delta at or below zero over the configured number of runs.
- An `ExperimentPlan`'s proposal digest is logged before any of its cells run, and cells trace to `SessionDiagnosis` evidence plus a stratified sample by a logged deterministic rule, never to an S-set priority.
- The knowledge ledger's `id@digest` entries and the composition manifest's occurrences agree; a ledger entry with no matching manifest occurrence is flagged as never having been in play.
- Persisted artefacts are hash-chained per checkpoint and signed daily manifests reach write-once storage, and a per-client crypto-shredding key exists before any client-scoped erasure request can be honored.

## Rollout

1. **Landed** — the `environment/run` stamp, the `verification/run` event, and the runner that appends both: every executed run of a standard, passing or failing, is durable with its executor and workspace tree hash, a certificate needs a fully passing run of its revision, trajectories carry the attempt count, and `@deepseek-ai/dsh-fleet` (`ctx.fleet`) runs the cells and folds a leaderboard per route and environment. The `EnvironmentStats` fold that W1 stage 2 and W3 stage 2 read is the scorekeeper's pass@k over the stamped batches; keying it by policy version waits for the stamp to carry one.
2. **Blocking** — the read barrier as filesystem and process authority. A validator-root fs-policy plugin, monotonic tool guards, implementer presets without a log-reading tool, and an invariant on certificates; until then every certificate measures only what the implementer could read.
3. **Blocking** — attributable decisions and pinned data-use terms. `signoff/recorded`, `decidedBy` with an argument digest on approvals, `dataUse/terms` at session creation, shipped redaction rules, and a curator that records rule hits; without them no client auditor can verify a gate and no transcript may become training data.
4. **Major** — content-addressed identity: component and skill digests, and the composition manifest event. Lineage, leaderboards per version, quarantine of dynamic packages, and the manifest-versus-ledger invariant all key on `id@digest`.
5. **Landed** — the scorekeeper as a session projection (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-scorekeeper`): the `sessionFacts` unit beside goal and verification, a scoreboard folded from persisted logs and partitioned by route, environment, isolation, and held-out split, pass@k over the stamped batches, and a JSONL facts export. What remains is the archive ledger — `HarnessVariant` records over storage with parents, operators, evaluations, and status — and the field groups whose producers do not exist yet.
6. **Landed** — the budget policy plugin (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-budget-policy`): token, wall-time, and cost caps from config, folded from the session log on `agent/pre-step`, a `budget/breach` event, and a durable goal block no round driver resumes; the model sees nothing because the step never opens. What remains is wiring per-cell caps from the fleet plan.
7. **Landed** — the experiment service (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-experiments`): a plan frozen by a content digest before any cell runs, both arms through the fleet at paired repetition indexes under `experiment-<digest>-<arm>` stamp groups, per-environment and pooled bootstrap intervals seeded from the digest, and a projected token budget refused loud. What remains is the staged ladder, cells derived by rule from diagnosis evidence, presets as a second arm dimension, and per-cell caps enforced during the run rather than projected.
8. **Major** — structured output for top-level presets as a plugin. Attach the structured-output runtime to a preset's agent context; Intake, Program service, and Trajectory Analyst get forced schemas with logged rejection paths.
9. **Major** — trainer operator, model registry, model lineage, environment factory, and admission. W3 end to end, including the Article 53 documentation generated from the lineage record.
10. **Minor** — the deny-capable monitor on the tool guard. Impact classes deny by default, ask for a bounded class, and log `oversight/deny`; makes deployment and secrets human gates.
11. **Minor** — durable orchestration. Deferred: cells are idempotent by header hash × environment × repetition and recover from persisted child sessions; a journaling workflow engine provider arrives with the program ledger.
12. **Minor** — a live run viewer fed by session logs and workflow events. The client's `ui-workflow-run` renders run, phase, and member status only today; a model's-eye view at any seq is the view no competitor can prove complete.

Shifts: the durable driver of an unattended fleet. Each district opens a slot on its cadence, freezes what the slot runs into a content digest, and records the whole shift as `shift/*` events in the slot's own session log. That ledger is the only thing a restarted process reads: it resumes an interrupted shift under the same identity, runs exactly the cells that never started, and refuses a slot whose district has already spent its window. =================== improvement/program
# @deepseek-ai/dsh-program
Programs: the durable ledger of one client deliverable decomposed into many goals. A program is a frozen spec, one program session holding `program/*` events, one department session and git worktree per goal, and one integration session whose certificate over the merged head is what a release claims. Every ledger event is appended after the fact it records is durable, so a restarted process reconciles each goal from its department's own log and worktree, never runs a department twice, never runs one integration twice, and never releases without a certificate. What a certificate covers is a commit: a session is certified only over a clean worktree, the ledger records the revision and tree it certified, and the integration merges a department branch only while that branch still points at it. A department is staffed either by the harness agent this service drives or, through the subagent seam, by an external coding agent whose attempts it records and whose tree it certifies. The [program-ledger](../../../.agents/notes/proposed/architecture/2026-09-06-program-ledger.md), [external-implementer](../../../.agents/notes/proposed/architecture/2026-09-06-program-external-implementer.md), and [workflow-integrity](../../../.agents/notes/proposed/architecture/2026-09-08-program-workflow-integrity.md) Agent Notes own the design rationale.

26:`record(agent, { transition, principal, artefactSha256, evidence })` validates every field, appends `signoff/recorded` to the agent's session, and returns the detached record. `latest(agent, transition)` folds the agent's own log for the newest record of one transition; the exported pure `latestSignoff(events, transition)` folds any log a consumer already holds — `@deepseek-ai/dsh-program` reads a program session that way, without an injection.
28:[Omitted long matching line]
30:Every refusal carries `SIGNOFF_INVALID_RECORD` and names the field at fault: an unknown transition, a digest that is not lowercase 64-hex, a principal that is not a person or names nobody, an empty display name, an evidence pointer that names nothing or exceeds the configured length, a list above `maxEvidence`, and a second signature of one transition over an artefact the session already signed another one for.
36:| `signoff/recorded` | Once per signature, at `record()` | `transition`, `principal`, `artefactSha256`, `evidence` |
38:The [persistence catalog](../../../docs/persistence-catalog.md) carries the payload's declaration. A transition may be signed again — a re-signature after new evidence — and the newest record is the one `latest` answers with; a second record naming another artefact is refused, because the two would disagree about what the transition covered.
42:`@deepseek-ai/dsh-signoff/invariant` checks what the log can show: the transition is one of the five, the digest is lowercase 64-hex, the principal is a person with a non-empty id and no empty display name, every evidence pointer names a kind and a ref, and no session signs one transition over two artefacts.
44:It cannot check anything outside the log: that the principal is the person named, that the digest addresses a real artefact, that the evidence refs resolve, or that the signer saw them. Making the id binding is the deployment's identity provider's job; this package states who the deployment said signed.
48:`@deepseek-ai/dsh-program` gates both of its `requireSignoff` transitions on records in the program session: `spec-freeze` before it opens a program, `release` before `program/end { outcome: released }`. The program id is derived from the spec digest, so a caller addresses the program session — and signs into it — before the program exists. Neither gate injects this service; both fold the persisted log through `latestSignoff`.
60:- **The principal is recorded, never authenticated** — nothing verifies that the id names the person who signed, so a deployment whose identity provider is a configuration string has an audit trail naming a role rather than a person. A signed-message or IdP method belongs with an identity provider this repository does not have.
61:- **The note's `role`, `method`, and `scope` fields are absent** — the [four-goal note](../../../.agents/notes/proposed/architecture/2026-09-05-four-goal-workflows.md) names a signer role vocabulary, a signing method, and a stage scope on `SignoffRecord`; they wait for a stage vocabulary and an identity provider to fill them, so a consumer needing the signer's role reads it from the transition and its own context.
63:- **Only `dsh-program` reads a signature** — the relaxation, review-acceptance, and training-data-release transitions have no in-repository consumer yet, so recording one is durable evidence that nothing currently gates on.
